Memory/Context
Sets the stage for the Agent. In Posit AI, you can do this with AGENTS.MD







AGENTS.md Objective
Description




Project Context
Describes the purpose of the project, project structure, data sources, key datasets, analytical units, domain knowledge, assumptions, preferred packages, reporting requirements, and links to supporting documentation.


Workflow Rules
Defines the preferred way work is performed, including coding standards, analysis workflow, package-development practices, reporting conventions, file organisation, reproducibility requirements, testing expectations, and references to STYLE.md.


Constraints
Specifies mandatory requirements and guardrails such as preserving raw data, maintaining backwards compatibility, using approved coordinate reference systems, handling sensitive data securely, avoiding destructive file operations, respecting database constraints, and documenting assumptions and limitations.

text:
LLMs … a few comments
LLMs can be surprisingly bad at things. The classic example (a year ago) was counting r’s in words

Let’s try now…

It is all good now. LLMs improved in the last year
But, let’s try a longer sentence that is a bit harder…
Rory the roaring raspberry rabbit raced round the rocky river, wrangling rambunctious robins in bright red raincoats.

# let's run in R ourselves...
x <-"Rory the roaring raspberry rabbit raced round the rocky river, wrangling rambunctious robins in bright red raincoats"

message( glue::glue("There are {crayon::red(stringr::str_count( tolower(x),'r'))} r's" ) )  

There are 19 r's









Note



Main Point: Be careful about judging LLMs solely on its “stupid-ish” moments. Often if you give it the right tools and context, it can often succeed. This leads to discussion on Agents.

text:
What is vibe-coding?
As with lots of terminology in the AI boom, defining vibe-coding is a bit nebulous. Different people (and bots!) use the term differently. For our purposes, let’s keep it simple:
Vibe-coding is a workflow where you describe what you want in natural language, an LLM writes the code, and you iteratively refine the result until you achieve the desired outcome in a reproducible way.

Strengths








Strength
Description




Reproducibility
R code records each transformation, parameter and analytical decision, making the spatial workflow easier to reproduce and audit.


Automation
A scripted workflow can be rerun when input data change, without manually repeating each GIS operation.


Scalability
The same analysis can be applied consistently across many species, sites, catchments or input files.


Reporting integration
Maps, figures, tables and results can be generated directly in a Quarto report.


Reuse
Repeated spatial operations can be converted into functions or incorporated into an R package.


Extensibility
Once the initial workflow works, it can be expanded with loops, simulations, databases, APIs and specialist spatial packages.

title: Module 3: Vibe-coding (with spatial data)

title: Module 3: Vibe-coding (with spatial data)
text:
Some final thoughts
Disclaimer: This is us free-thinking in real time during a paradign shift. Feel free to disagree or contribute your own thoughts.

Resist intellectual laziness
This is not a flippant statement.
As AI tools become more capable, there is a risk that we outsource not only the coding, but also the thinking.
Contributing factors:

We are increasingly time-stressed.
Projects often have unrealistic deadlines.
Vibe-coding can create psychological distance from the underlying problem.
Modern digital platforms reward speed, visibility, and confidence more than deep understanding.
AI can produce plausible outputs that reduce the incentive to question assumptions or verify results.

Key message: The danger is not that AI writes code. The danger is that we stop engaging critically with the problem we are trying to solve.


Reviewing the code

Despite the temptation, we are going to need to be disciplined about reading the code and ensure that we understand exactly what it is doing.
Not all code requires the same level of assessment (importing data vs ggplot vs statistical analysis)
Learning how to QC/QA your code and outputs will increase in importance
As noted, I have a STYLE.MD guide that writes the code in my style. That helps me review/evaluate the code quicker.



Learning from vibe-coding

New approaches to tackling a problem (plan mode)
Reading the code that the Agent wrote introduced me to new functions/approaches to making new maps



Beyond spatial data

Obviously, vibe-coding is not restricted to spatial data and you can implement the same approach to other type of data.



Homogensing workflow (the future)
An emerging question that we are wondering about (and we mentioned in module 1…sorry to dwell) is what does this mean for how we tackle these steps in the future and our workflows.
How homogenized do our workflows become?

Standardised ARI STYLE.MD, WOKFLOW.MD, and set of SKILLS.MD files/folders.

Do we have a project folder that has a similar structure so both humans and a local LLM that has been trained on our workflow can easily understand it, revise, and QC it?

All of this seems apt given all the discussion on templates/standardisation


“The Castle” references feel rather appropriate at this point in time…

text:
Steps using Posit AI (aka Posit Assistant)
Let’s walk through a workflow…

Step 1: set-up the project folder with the data
I have already created a folder download project setup for Agent
Let’s have a look around the folder as there are few things in there that I added from the Copilot approach above.
The basic structure of the project folder is …


Let’s have a look at the agent file…(snapshot of the top)

And the spatial_analyst skill…(snapshot of the top)



Step 2: Use plan mode
Before diving into getting the spatial code, you need to have an idea/plan of what you want the Agent to do. The ‘plan mode’ can be useful for this.

PROMPT
/plan (sets to plan mode)
I need to create a png map using an R workflow. I have a graph (figures/qgis_goal.png) that I want you to replicate. I first want to create a plan that we argue on to create similar map output (‘figures/rmap.png’) and all points will be data/spatial/vmfrp_wallpolla_veg.gpkg. A basemap and Victorian layer will be needed to be found. See .posit/AGENTS.MD ‘.posit/spatial_analyst/’ skill to guide workflow approach. During the planning stage, do not guess what I want but rather ask me explicitly. Save the plan as PLAN.MD in base directory.

Run plan mode…

We will work through this live. An example of what might come out is shown below:


MD files are Markdown and very commonly used in programming world as they are a balance between between .txt file with no formatting and Word doc (excessive formatting😊). See Intro to Markdown



Step 3: Execute the plan
Okay, we got a plan and told AI what we want. Let’s implement the plan and see how it does. I will mostly go YOLO ( You Only Look Once). I want to see what it can do.
I will run Claude Sonnet 5.0 for the example here.


Step 4: Review the results
Let’s walk through some of the outputs.
Initial draft…



Step 5: Iterate (as needed)
It is very likely the output is not quite there (or worse)…

Given that we have the qgis_main.png as the goal, let’s have AI assess itself and see if it can do better.

PROMPT
/plan (sets to plan mode)
Using the qgis_goal.png, compare and contrast to mapVegSites.png and provide a list of changes needed to mapVegSites.png to make it match better.
